question: There were continual failures in Spain’s online system for precautionary monitoring of gender-based violence — ‘anti-abuse bracelets’ — for at least eight months in 2024, following a change in service provider. The courts received notifications that no new devices could be installed and defective ones could not be replaced, thus jeopardising the safety of numerous victims.
Spain’s Public Prosecutor’s Office has acknowledged that this led to cases against abusers being dismissed or dropped.

Several pieces of EU legislation may have been violated: Directive 2012/29/EU, which requires effective protection measures to be guaranteed; Directive 2011/99/EU on the European protection order, which requires the devices to be reliable; Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement of essential services; and Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence, which is in the process of being transposed.
In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the Spanish Government has established the necessary guarantees and mechanisms to comply with European protection standards in a timely manner?
Will the Commission ensure that such a state of affairs is prevented and will not reoccur?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.1.2026) Barring orders are covered by Article 19 of the Violence Against Women Directive1. Recital 46 of the Directive allows Member States to make this possible, where relevant, available, appropriate and given the circumstances of the case, through electronic monitoring.

Where electronic monitoring is used, victims should always be informed about its capabilities and limitations. Member States have until June 2027 to transpose the Directive, following which the Commission will conduct transposition checks. The Victims’ Rights Directive2 provides for a set of rights for all victims of crime, including victims of gender-based violence.

The proposed revision of the Victims’ Rights Directive3 on which the co-legislators have recently reached a provisional agreement will further strengthen those rights, including ensuring victims’ physical protection. The Commission is monitoring the state of implementation of the Victims’ Rights Directive in all Member States, including in Spain4.

According to the Commission, the Spanish law fully transposes the victims’ rights legislation into national law. In addition, the European Protection Order Directive5 allows for protection measures for persons in danger taken in one Member State to be recognised by another Member State in order to continue the protection of such persons when they travel or move to another EU Member State.
The specificities of national protection orders and the tools to enforce these, remain the responsibility of Member States.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on combating

violence against women and domestic violence, OJ L, 2024/1385, 24.5.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1385/oj. 2 Directive 2012/29/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA, OJ L 315, 14.11.2012, p. 57.

3 Proposal for a Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Directive 2012/29/EU establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA, COM/2023/424 final. Co-legislators reached a provisional political agreement on the proposal on 10 December 2025.

4 In particular, the Commission has analysed whether Member States have completely transposed into national legislation all normative provisions of the Victims’ Rights Directive. 5 Directive 2011/99/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the European protection order, OJ L 338, 21.12.2011, p. 2.
